introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0770 Pure Maths With Statistics 1, June 2022, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL questions: Section A is Pure Mathematics (questions 1 to 35) and Section B is Statistics (questions 36 to 50). Formulae booklets and calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one answer you score zero). Avoid spending too much time on any one question. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room.
incertitudes: Le sujet est un scan sans couche texte (6 pages ; page de garde conforme : ADVANCED LEVEL, 0770 Pure Maths With Statistics 1, JUNE 2022, QCM d'une heure et demie ; filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés), lu page par page en image puis relu en recadrages agrandis (jusqu'à 400 dpi). Aucun corrigé ni clé officiels : tous les corrigés sont rédigés et chaque valeur numérique recalculée par script (sympy sous Anaconda). Le sujet compte bien 50 questions (35 de Pure Mathematics, 15 de Statistics), toutes obligatoires. Aucune figure imprimée n'est nécessaire.

Question 17 : la période de sin(2x/3) vaut 3 pi ; aucune des options imprimées (4pi/3, 2pi/3, 3pi/4, 3pi/2) ne convient. Convertie en question ouverte, aucune clé n'est affirmée (la fonction visée était peut-être sin(3x/2), de période 4pi/3, option A, mais ce n'est qu'une hypothèse).

Question 24 : le scan est dégradé ; le signe avant j dans le point de la première droite (« 3i ? j + k ») et le signe avant k dans sa direction (« i + 2j ? k ») sont illisibles (glyphe proche de ÷). Lus comme « - » dans les deux cas : avec « 3i + j + k » le système donne lambda = 4/3, absent des options, alors que la lecture « 3i - j + k » donne lambda = 2, mu = -1 avec la composante k concordante (option B). Donnée reconstituée, signalée entre crochets dans l'énoncé et dans le corrigé.

Question 50 : l'énoncé imprimé porte « (X) = 5/3 » (la lettre E est tombée dans le scan) ; lu comme E(X) = 5/3, ce que le calcul confirme (E(X) = 70/42). Var(X) = 5/9 = 0,5556, arrondi 0,56 (option C) ; l'option A (0,55) est une troncature.

Question 49 : la covariance est calculée avec le diviseur n (3,4167 donc 3,42, option A) ; avec n - 1 on obtiendrait 4,1, absent des options. Les options C et D sont imprimées identiquement (4,31), toutes deux fausses.

Question 20 : les options A et C sont imprimées identiquement (i - 2j - k), toutes deux fausses ; la clé B est unique. Question 6 : la clé A est la seule dont le dénominateur est 5! 3! 2! (A 5 fois, R 3 fois, B 2 fois).

Question 10 : les ensembles sont imprimés avec le symbole de réunion à la place de « ou » (« {x : x < -2 U 1 < x < 3} ») ; transcrit tel quel, option A. Question 32 : le logarithme est décimal (a = 10^1,3 = 19,95).

Question 41 : la ligne des fréquences du tableau est dédoublée par le bruit du scan ; lue 3, 4, 5, 5, 2, 1 (somme 20), ce qui donne la moyenne 5,2 de l'option C : lecture cohérente avec une option imprimée. Plusieurs options (1/5, 1/2, 2/3...) portent des traces de bruit de numérisation sans effet sur la lecture.

Questions 17, 29 et 31 relues à 400 dpi : lectures confirmées (sin(2x/3), exposant 1/2 dans (1 + x/2)^(1/2), terme k/2^(r-1)). Les remarques sur les distracteurs dans les corrigés sont des explications plausibles des erreurs, pas des données du sujet.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

The remainder when the polynomial $f(x)=2x^3+ax^2-3x+1$ is divided by $(x+1)$ is $-2$. The value of the constant $a$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: By the remainder theorem the remainder on division by $(x+1)$ is $f(-1)$. $f(-1)=2(-1)^3+a(-1)^2-3(-1)+1=-2+a+3+1=a+2$. Setting $a+2=-2$ gives $a=-4$. Check: $f(x)=2x^3-4x^2-3x+1$, $f(-1)=-2-4+3+1=-2$. The other options come from sign slips when evaluating $f(-1)$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the roots of the equation $2x^2+5x-3=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$, then the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For $2x^2+5x-3=0$: $\alpha+\beta=-\dfrac52$ and $\alpha\beta=-\dfrac32$. Then $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta=\dfrac{25}{4}+3=\dfrac{37}{4}$. Check with the actual roots $\tfrac12$ and $-3$: $\tfrac14+9=\tfrac{37}{4}$. Option C ($\tfrac{25}{4}$) is only $(\alpha+\beta)^2$, forgetting the term $-2\alpha\beta$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\dfrac{x+1}{(x-3)(x-5)}\equiv\dfrac{M}{x-3}+\dfrac{N}{x-5}$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply by $(x-3)(x-5)$: $x+1\equiv M(x-5)+N(x-3)$. Put $x=3$: $4=-2M$, so $M=-2$. Put $x=5$: $6=2N$, so $N=3$. Check: $\dfrac{-2(x-5)+3(x-3)}{(x-3)(x-5)}=\dfrac{x+1}{(x-3)(x-5)}$. Option A has the wrong sign for $M$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solution set of the inequality $|2x-1|>3$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $|2x-1|>3$ means $2x-1>3$ or $2x-1<-3$. The first gives $x>2$; the second gives $2x<-2$, so $x<-1$. The solution set is $\{x: x<-1 \text{ or } x>2\}$. Check: $x=3$ gives $|5|=5>3$; $x=0$ gives $|-1|=1<3$. Option C, $-1<x<2$, is the solution of the reverse inequality $|2x-1|<3$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A partial order relation is that which is
questions.corrige_markdown: A partial order on a set is, by definition, reflexive, anti-symmetric and transitive (example: $\le$ on $\mathbb{R}$). A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive is an equivalence relation (A), not a partial order. B and D each omit one of the three required properties (transitivity, reflexivity). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of distinct arrangements of the letters of the word $ABRACADABRAR$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The word has 12 letters: $A$ appears 5 times (positions 1, 4, 6, 8, 11), $B$ twice, $R$ three times (positions 3, 10, 12), and $C$ and $D$ once each. Total $5+2+3+1+1=12$. The number of distinct arrangements is $\dfrac{12!}{5!\,2!\,3!}$, which equals $\dfrac{12!}{5!\,3!\,2!}$ (option A) since the order of the factors does not matter. Numerically $\dfrac{12!}{5!\,3!\,2!}=332\,640$. Option B would need three $B$'s, C two $R$'s, and D four $B$'s. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is given by $f(x)=ax+b$. If $f(3)=3$ and $f(4)=5$, then the values of the constants are such that
The value of $2\log_4 8$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $\log_4 8=\dfrac{\ln 8}{\ln 4}=\dfrac{3\ln 2}{2\ln 2}=\dfrac32$. Hence $2\log_4 8=3$. Check: $4^{3/2}=8$. Option B ($\tfrac32$) is $\log_4 8$ without the factor 2. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $u_n=5+\dfrac32(n-1)$ is the $n$th term of an arithmetic progression, the sum of the first twenty terms of this progression is
questions.corrige_markdown: The first term is $a=u_1=5$ and the common difference is $d=\tfrac32$. $S_{20}=\dfrac{20}{2}\big[2a+19d\big]=10\Big[10+19\cdot\dfrac32\Big]=10(10+28.5)=385$. Check with $S_n=\dfrac n2(u_1+u_{20})$: $u_{20}=5+28.5=33.5$, so $S_{20}=10(5+33.5)=385$. Option A (770) forgets the factor $\tfrac12$ in the sum formula. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solution set of the inequality $\dfrac{(1-x)(x-3)}{(x+2)}>0$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The critical values are $x=-2$ (denominator, excluded), $x=1$ and $x=3$. Sign of $\dfrac{(1-x)(x-3)}{x+2}$: for $x<-2$ the numerator is $(+)(-)=-$ and the denominator $-$, so the quotient is $+$. For $-2<x<1$: numerator $-$, denominator $+$, quotient $-$. For $1<x<3$: numerator $(-)(-)=+$, denominator $+$, quotient $+$. For $x>3$: numerator $(-)(+)=-$, denominator $+$, quotient $-$. The quotient is positive for $x<-2$ or $1<x<3$. Check: $x=-3$ gives $\frac{(4)(-6)}{-1}=24>0$; $x=2$ gives $\frac{(-1)(-1)}{4}>0$; $x=0$ gives $\frac{3\cdot(-3)}{2}<0$. This is option A (printed with the union sign standing for \"or\"). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $p$ and $q$ are two statements. The compound statement $p\Rightarrow q$ is false when
questions.corrige_markdown: An implication $p\Rightarrow q$ is false in exactly one case: the hypothesis $p$ is true and the conclusion $q$ is false. It is true when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth value (A and D describe true cases), and being converses of each other (B) says nothing about the truth value of $p\Rightarrow q$. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: $p$ and $q$ have the same truth value
$p$ and $q$ are converse of each other

questions.enonce_markdown: If $a+bi=\dfrac{1+i}{1-2i}$, the values of the constants $a$ and $b$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $1+2i$: $\dfrac{(1+i)(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)}=\dfrac{1+2i+i+2i^2}{1+4}=\dfrac{-1+3i}{5}$. So $a=-\dfrac15$ and $b=\dfrac35$. Option A has the wrong sign for the real part ($1+2i^2=-1$, not $+1$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $x^2-4x+9\equiv(x+A)^2+B$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Complete the square: $x^2-4x+9=(x-2)^2-4+9=(x-2)^2+5$. Comparing with $(x+A)^2+B$ gives $A=-2$ and $B=5$. Expanding $(x-2)^2+5=x^2-4x+9$ confirms it. Options A and B take $A=+2$, forgetting that $(x+A)^2$ has middle term $+2Ax$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two variables $y$ and $x$ are connected by the equation $y=a(x+2)^k$. A linear equivalence of this equation is
questions.corrige_markdown: Take logarithms: $\log y=\log a+\log (x+2)^k=k\log(x+2)+\log a$. This is of the form $Y=mX+c$ with $Y=\log y$, $X=\log(x+2)$, gradient $k$ and intercept $\log a$. Option A wrongly writes $\log k(x+2)$, B swaps the roles of $a$ and $k$, and C replaces $x+2$ by $2x$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If matrix $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&k&2\\2&-6&0\\1&-2&-4\end{pmatrix}$, then the value of $k$ for which $|\mathbf{A}|=4$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Expand along the first row: $|\mathbf{A}|=-1\begin{vmatrix}-6&0\\-2&-4\end{vmatrix}-k\begin{vmatrix}2&0\\1&-4\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}2&-6\\1&-2\end{vmatrix}=-1(24)-k(-8)+2(-4+6)=-24+8k+4=8k-20$. Setting $8k-20=4$ gives $k=3$. Check with $k=3$: $-24+24+4=4$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, where $f(x)=\ln(4+x^2)$, then the value of $f'(2)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: By the chain rule $f'(x)=\dfrac{2x}{4+x^2}$. Hence $f'(2)=\dfrac{4}{4+4}=\dfrac12$. Option A ($\tfrac14$) comes from using $2$ instead of $2x$ in the numerator. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The period of the trigonometric function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, where $f(x)=\sin\dfrac23 x$ is

*Options as printed:* A) $\dfrac43\pi$   B) $\dfrac23\pi$   C) $\dfrac34\pi$   D) $\dfrac32\pi$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The function $\sin(\omega x)$ has period $\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$. Here $\omega=\dfrac23$, so the period is $2\pi\times\dfrac32=3\pi$. Check: $\sin\!\big(\tfrac23(x+3\pi)\big)=\sin\!\big(\tfrac23x+2\pi\big)=\sin\tfrac23x$, and no smaller positive shift works. The correct value $3\pi$ is not among the printed options (A $\tfrac43\pi$, B $\tfrac23\pi$, C $\tfrac34\pi$, D $\tfrac32\pi$), so the question cannot be marked automatically.

**Answer: $3\pi$ (not listed).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: If a polynomial $P(x)$ produces a quotient $(x^2+2x+1)$ and a remainder $5$ when divided by $(x+1)$, then $P(x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Dividend $=$ divisor $\times$ quotient $+$ remainder: $P(x)=(x+1)(x^2+2x+1)+5=x^3+2x^2+x+x^2+2x+1+5=x^3+3x^2+3x+6$. Check: $P(-1)=-1+3-3+6=5$, the stated remainder. The other options come from mistakes when collecting terms. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The parametric equations of a curve are $1-x=\tan\theta$ and $y=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$. The cartesian equation of this curve is
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta$. Here $y=\sec\theta$ and $\tan\theta=1-x$, so $y^2=1+(1-x)^2=1+1-2x+x^2=x^2-2x+2$. Rearranged: $x^2-y^2-2x+2=0$. Check at $\theta=0$: $x=1$, $y=1$ gives $1-1-2+2=0$. Options A, B and D have a wrong middle term (a mistake in expanding $(1-x)^2$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the cartesian equation of a plane is $x-2y+z-5=0$, then the vector normal to this plane is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a plane $ax+by+cz=d$ the vector $a\mathbf{i}+b\mathbf{j}+c\mathbf{k}$ is normal to it. Here $a=1$, $b=-2$, $c=1$, so a normal vector is $\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}$ (option B). Options A and C are printed identically ($\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}$) and both have the wrong sign on $\mathbf{k}$; D has the wrong sign on $\mathbf{j}$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Some values of the function $f$ are given in the table below:

| $x$ | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $f(x)$ | 5 | 15 | 28 | $k$ |

If by the trapezium rule $\displaystyle\int_2^5 f(x)\,dx\approx 68$, then the value of the constant $k$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: There are 4 ordinates, so 3 strips of width $h=1$. Trapezium rule: $\displaystyle\int_2^5 f\,dx\approx\dfrac h2\big[y_0+y_3+2(y_1+y_2)\big]=\dfrac12\big[5+k+2(15+28)\big]=\dfrac{91+k}{2}$. Setting $\dfrac{91+k}{2}=68$ gives $91+k=136$, so $k=45$. Check: $\tfrac12(5+45+86)=68$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $x_1$ is a first approximate root of the equation $f(x)=0$. By Newton - Raphson's procedure, a second approximate root of this equation is given by
questions.corrige_markdown: The tangent to $y=f(x)$ at $x_1$ is $y-f(x_1)=f'(x_1)(x-x_1)$. It meets the $x$-axis ($y=0$) at $x=x_1-\dfrac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)}$. This is the Newton - Raphson formula $x_2=x_1-\dfrac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)}$. Options A and B invert the fraction; B and D have the wrong sign. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\dfrac{2x-3}{x+1}$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq-1$, the value of $f^{-1}(0)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $f^{-1}(0)$ is the value of $x$ such that $f(x)=0$. $\dfrac{2x-3}{x+1}=0\Rightarrow 2x-3=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac32$ (and $x\ne-1$). Check: $f(\tfrac32)=\dfrac{0}{5/2}=0$. Option A has the wrong sign; C and D are the reciprocal values. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$ for which the lines $\mathbf{r}=3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}+\lambda(\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k})$ [the signs before $\mathbf{j}$ in the point and before $\mathbf{k}$ in the direction are smudged in the scan; read as $-$ and $-$] and $\mathbf{r}=4\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}+\mu(-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k})$ intersect are
questions.corrige_markdown: Equate components (with the lines as read above). $\mathbf{i}$: $3+\lambda=4-\mu$. $\mathbf{j}$: $-1+2\lambda=4+\mu$. Adding: $2+3\lambda=8$, so $\lambda=2$, and then $\mu=1-\lambda=-1$. Check the $\mathbf{k}$ component: $1-\lambda=1-2=-1$ and $1+2\mu=1-2=-1$. They agree, so the lines intersect at $(5,3,-1)$ with $\lambda=2$, $\mu=-1$. Option A has the right $\lambda$ but the wrong sign of $\mu$. [With the sign before $\mathbf{j}$ read as $+$ the system would give $\lambda=\tfrac43$, which is in no option; the $-$ reading is the one consistent with the options.] **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of ways of arranging 5 girls on a bench if the two left-handed girls must sit together is
questions.corrige_markdown: Treat the two left-handed girls as one block. There are then $4$ objects (the block and the other 3 girls), arranged in $4!=24$ ways. Inside the block the two girls can swap places in $2!=2$ ways. Total $=24\times2=48$. Option A (24) forgets the internal arrangement of the block; D (96) doubles the correct value. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\sin\!\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin\!\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $\sin A-\sin B=2\cos\dfrac{A+B}{2}\sin\dfrac{A-B}{2}$. With $A=x+\tfrac\pi6$, $B=x-\tfrac\pi6$: $\dfrac{A+B}{2}=x$ and $\dfrac{A-B}{2}=\dfrac\pi6$, so the difference is $2\cos x\sin\dfrac\pi6=2\cos x\cdot\dfrac12=\cos x$. Check by expanding: $\sin x\cos\tfrac\pi6+\cos x\sin\tfrac\pi6-\sin x\cos\tfrac\pi6+\cos x\sin\tfrac\pi6=2\cos x\sin\tfrac\pi6=\cos x$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The graph of $y=\dfrac{4}{x^2-1}$ has
questions.corrige_markdown: The denominator vanishes at $x^2=1$, i.e. $x=\pm1$, where the numerator is $4\neq0$: two vertical asymptotes $x=\pm1$. As $x\to\pm\infty$, $y=\dfrac{4}{x^2-1}\to0$, so $y=0$ is a horizontal asymptote. Option C ($y=4$) confuses the numerator with the limit; A denies the horizontal asymptote; B misses the asymptote $x=-1$. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: two vertical asymptotes $x=\pm1$ and no horizontal asymptote
one vertical asymptote $x=1$ and one horizontal asymptote $y=0$
two vertical asymptotes $x=\pm1$ and a horizontal asymptote $y=4$
two vertical asymptotes $x=\pm1$ and a horizontal asymptote $y=0$

questions.enonce_markdown: Given the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}-2xy=0$. If $y=1$ when $x=1$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Separate the variables: $\dfrac{dy}{y}=2x\,dx$. Integrate: $\ln y=x^2+c$, so $y=Ae^{x^2}$. Use $y=1$ at $x=1$: $1=Ae$, so $A=e^{-1}$. Therefore $y=e^{x^2-1}$. Check: $y'=2xe^{x^2-1}=2xy$ and $y(1)=e^0=1$. Option C ignores the condition ($A=1$ gives $y(1)=e$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The coefficient of $x^2$ in the binomial expansion of $\left(1+\dfrac12x\right)^{\frac12}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For $(1+u)^{n}$ with $n=\tfrac12$ the $u^2$ term is $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2!}u^2=\dfrac{\frac12\cdot(-\frac12)}{2}u^2=-\dfrac18u^2$. With $u=\tfrac12x$, $u^2=\tfrac14x^2$, so the coefficient of $x^2$ is $-\dfrac18\cdot\dfrac14=-\dfrac1{32}$. Check: $(1+\tfrac x2)^{1/2}=1+\tfrac x4-\tfrac{x^2}{32}+\cdots$. Option A has the wrong sign; B forgets to square the factor $\tfrac12$ in $u=\tfrac12x$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The coordinates of the points where the curves $y=2x-3$ and $y=x^2-2x$ intersect are
questions.corrige_markdown: Equate the $y$ values: $x^2-2x=2x-3\Rightarrow x^2-4x+3=0\Rightarrow(x-1)(x-3)=0$, so $x=1$ or $x=3$. Then $y=2x-3$ gives $y=-1$ and $y=3$. The points are $(1,-1)$ and $(3,3)$. Check in $y=x^2-2x$: $1-2=-1$ and $9-6=3$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of the constant $k$ for which $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\left(\dfrac{k}{2^{r-1}}\right)=10$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The terms are $k,\ \dfrac k2,\ \dfrac k4,\dots$: a geometric series with first term $k$ and common ratio $\tfrac12$ ($|r|<1$, so it converges). $S_\infty=\dfrac{k}{1-\frac12}=2k$. Setting $2k=10$ gives $k=5$. Check: $5(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\cdots)=5\times2=10$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If a linear reduction of the relationship $y=ax^n$ produced the result $\log y=2\log x+1.3$, then $a$ and $n$ are such that
questions.corrige_markdown: Taking logs of $y=ax^n$: $\log y=n\log x+\log a$. Comparing with $\log y=2\log x+1.3$: $n=2$ (the gradient) and $\log a=1.3$, so $a=10^{1.3}=19.95\approx20$ (logarithms to base 10). Check: $20x^2$ gives $\log y=\log20+2\log x=1.301+2\log x$. Options with $a\approx2$ read $1.3$ as if it were $a$ or $\log a\approx0.3$, and options with $n=20$ confuse $n$ with $a$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The complex number $z$, in the form $a+bi$, for which $(1-2i)z=3-i$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $z=\dfrac{3-i}{1-2i}=\dfrac{(3-i)(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)}=\dfrac{3+6i-i-2i^2}{5}=\dfrac{5+5i}{5}=1+i$. Check: $(1-2i)(1+i)=1+i-2i-2i^2=3-i$. Option A has the wrong sign on the imaginary part. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of $a$ for which the quadratic equation $2x^2-6x+3a=0$ has equal roots is
questions.corrige_markdown: Equal roots require the discriminant $b^2-4ac=0$. Here the coefficients are $2$, $-6$ and $3a$: $36-4(2)(3a)=36-24a=0$, so $a=\dfrac{36}{24}=\dfrac32$. Check: with $a=\tfrac32$ the equation is $2x^2-6x+\tfrac92=2\big(x-\tfrac32\big)^2=0$, a perfect square. Options A and B are the inverse of the correct value. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{x}{1+2x^2}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator ($\tfrac{d}{dx}(1+2x^2)=4x$): $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{1+2x^2}dx=\dfrac14\ln(1+2x^2)+C$. Then $\Big[\dfrac14\ln(1+2x^2)\Big]_1^2=\dfrac14(\ln 9-\ln 3)=\dfrac14\ln 3$. Numerical check: both the integral and $\tfrac14\ln3$ equal about $0.2747$. Option B ($\tfrac12\ln3$) comes from using $\tfrac12$ instead of $\tfrac14$ as the constant factor. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: STATISTICS**

Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=\dfrac35$, $P(B)=\dfrac{3}{10}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac45$. What is the probability that both $A$ and $B$ will occur?
questions.corrige_markdown: Addition rule: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. So $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac35+\dfrac3{10}-\dfrac45=\dfrac{6+3-8}{10}=\dfrac1{10}$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A discrete random variable $X$ has probability mass function $f$, where $f(x)=k(x-1)$ for $x=2,3,4$ and $f(x)=0$ otherwise. The value of constant $k$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The probabilities must sum to 1: $k(1)+k(2)+k(3)=6k=1$, so $k=\dfrac16$. Check: $\tfrac16+\tfrac26+\tfrac36=1$. Option C ($\tfrac13$) is what one gets by counting only two of the three values ($3k=1$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The probability density function $f$ of a continuous variable $X$ is given by $f(x)=\dfrac23(x-2)$ for $3\le x\le4$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x<3$ and $x>4$. The mean of this distribution is
questions.corrige_markdown: First check that $f$ is a density: $\displaystyle\int_3^4\tfrac23(x-2)dx=\tfrac13\big[(x-2)^2\big]_3^4=\tfrac13(4-1)=1$. The mean is $E(X)=\displaystyle\int_3^4x\cdot\tfrac23(x-2)dx=\tfrac23\int_3^4(x^2-2x)dx=\tfrac23\Big[\tfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\Big]_3^4=\tfrac23\Big[\big(\tfrac{64}{3}-16\big)-(9-9)\Big]=\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac{16}{3}=\dfrac{32}{9}$ ($\approx3.56$, inside $[3,4]$ as it must be). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A random variable has a binomial probability distribution with mean $2$ and variance $1.6$. The values of the parameters $n$ and $p$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: For $X\sim B(n,p)$: mean $np=2$ and variance $npq=1.6$. Dividing, $q=\dfrac{1.6}{2}=0.8$, so $p=1-q=0.2$ and $n=\dfrac{2}{0.2}=10$. Check: $npq=10(0.2)(0.8)=1.6$. Options A and C swap $p$ and $q$ ($p=0.8$ would give a mean of $8$ for $n=10$ and $6.4$ for $n=8$). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Accidents occurring at a particular road junction happen randomly at an average rate of $2$ per week. The probability that exactly $2$ accidents will occur at this junction within a period of two weeks is
questions.corrige_markdown: Accidents occurring randomly at a constant rate follow a Poisson distribution. For two weeks the mean is $\lambda=2\times2=4$. $P(X=2)=\dfrac{e^{-4}\,4^2}{2!}=8e^{-4}\approx0.1465$. Option A ($2e^{-2}$) is the probability for a single week ($\lambda=2$: $\frac{e^{-2}2^2}{2!}=2e^{-2}$), the trap of ignoring the two-week period. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The frequency distribution of a data set is as shown below.

| $x$ | 1 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 9 | 11 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $f$ | 3 | 4 | 5 | 5 | 2 | 1 |

The mean of these data is
questions.corrige_markdown: $\sum f=3+4+5+5+2+1=20$ and $\sum fx=3(1)+4(3)+5(5)+5(7)+2(9)+1(11)=3+12+25+35+18+11=104$. Mean $=\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}=\dfrac{104}{20}=5.2$. The other options come from slips in the products $fx$ or in $\sum f$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A cooking gas bottling company claims that each bottle contains averagely $12.5$ kg of gas. Following complaints from the consumers of this product that they are being cheated, a hypothesis test is to be conducted to verify the claim. The null hypothesis $H_0$ and the alternative hypothesis $H_1$ for this test are
questions.corrige_markdown: The null hypothesis is the company's claim, $H_0:\mu=12.5$. Consumers say they are cheated, i.e. the bottles contain **less** gas than claimed, so the alternative is the one-tailed $H_1:\mu<12.5$. Option A tests for more than $12.5$ kg, and B and C put the value $12.5$ itself in $H_1$ (with $\ge$ or $\le$), which overlaps $H_0$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the regression lines of $y$ on $x$ and $x$ on $y$ are $y=0.72-0.49x$ and $x=0.65-0.25y$ respectively, then the product moment correlation coefficient between $x$ and $y$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The gradient of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $b_{yx}=-0.49$ and that of $x$ on $y$ is $b_{xy}=-0.25$. Then $r^2=b_{yx}\,b_{xy}=0.49\times0.25=0.1225$, so $|r|=0.35$. Both regression coefficients are negative, hence $r$ is negative: $r=-0.35$. Options A and D ignore the sign; B ($-0.68$) is not $\sqrt{0.1225}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Four competitors were ranked by two juries as shown below.

| Jury A | 2 | 1 | 4 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jury B | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |

The Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between the juries is
questions.corrige_markdown: Differences $d=A-B$: $1,\,-1,\,1,\,-1$, so $\sum d^2=4$. With $n=4$: $r_s=1-\dfrac{6\sum d^2}{n(n^2-1)}=1-\dfrac{6\times4}{4\times15}=1-\dfrac{24}{60}=\dfrac35$. Option B ($\tfrac25$) is the value of $\dfrac{6\sum d^2}{n(n^2-1)}$ itself, i.e. forgetting to subtract it from $1$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: For two events $A$ and $B$, $P(A)=\dfrac x2$, $P(B)=\dfrac x3$ and $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac23$, $0\le x\le1$. If $A$ and $B$ are independent, then the value of $x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Independence gives $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)=\dfrac{x^2}{6}$. Then $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac x2+\dfrac x3-\dfrac{x^2}{6}=\dfrac23$. Multiply by 6: $3x+2x-x^2=4$, i.e. $x^2-5x+4=0$, $(x-1)(x-4)=0$. Since $0\le x\le1$, $x=1$ (the root $x=4$ is rejected). Check: $P(A)=\tfrac12$, $P(B)=\tfrac13$, $P(A\cup B)=\tfrac12+\tfrac13-\tfrac16=\tfrac23$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A discrete random variable $X$ takes the values $1,2,3,4$ and $5$. If $P(X=1)=P(X=2)=\dfrac1{10}$ and $P(X=3)=P(X=4)=P(X=5)$, then the value of $P(X=4)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Let $P(X=3)=P(X=4)=P(X=5)=p$. The probabilities sum to 1: $\dfrac1{10}+\dfrac1{10}+3p=1$, so $3p=\dfrac45$ and $p=\dfrac{4}{15}$. Hence $P(X=4)=\dfrac4{15}$. Check: $\tfrac{2}{10}+\tfrac{12}{15}=\tfrac15+\tfrac45=1$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A continuous random variable has probability density function $f(x)=k(2+x)(2-x)$ for $0<x<2$ and $f(x)=0$ elsewhere. The value of constant $k$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $f(x)=k(4-x^2)$ and the total area must be 1: $\displaystyle\int_0^2k(4-x^2)dx=k\Big[4x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\Big]_0^2=k\Big(8-\dfrac83\Big)=\dfrac{16k}{3}=1$. So $k=\dfrac3{16}$. Option A ($\tfrac38$) is double the correct value. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the mean of a set of $4$ numbers is $5$ and the mean of another set of $3$ numbers is $12$, then the mean of the combined set of $7$ numbers is
questions.corrige_markdown: Sum of the first set $=4\times5=20$; sum of the second set $=3\times12=36$. Combined sum $=56$ over $7$ numbers, so the mean is $\dfrac{56}{7}=8$. Note that the simple average $\tfrac{5+12}{2}=8.5$ is not the weighted mean. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The following information is obtained from a bivariate data $(x,y)$.

| statistic | $\sum x$ | $\sum y$ | $\sum xy$ | $n$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| value | 21 | 43 | 171 | 6 |

The covariance for these data is
questions.corrige_markdown: With divisor $n$: $\operatorname{cov}(x,y)=\dfrac{\sum xy}{n}-\bar x\,\bar y=\dfrac{171}{6}-\dfrac{21}{6}\cdot\dfrac{43}{6}=28.5-25.083=3.4167\approx3.42$. This is option A. (With divisor $n-1$ the value would be $4.1$, which is in no option.) Options C and D are printed identically ($4.31$) and both are wrong. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$ is given in the table below.

| $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $P(X=x)$ | $\frac1{21}$ | $\frac5{14}$ | $\frac{10}{21}$ | $\frac5{42}$ |

If $E(X)=\dfrac53$ [the letter $E$ is missing in the scan, which prints \"(X) = 5/3\"], then $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Over the common denominator $42$ the probabilities are $\tfrac2{42},\tfrac{15}{42},\tfrac{20}{42},\tfrac5{42}$ (sum $1$). $E(X)=\dfrac{0+15+40+15}{42}=\dfrac{70}{42}=\dfrac53$, which confirms the given mean. $E(X^2)=\dfrac{0+15+80+45}{42}=\dfrac{140}{42}=\dfrac{10}{3}$. $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2=\dfrac{10}{3}-\dfrac{25}{9}=\dfrac59=0.5555\ldots\approx0.56$ (2 d.p.). Option A (0.55) truncates instead of rounding. **Answer: C.**
